text: From this there follows a further praise, which Johnson delivers with his customary plainness: "Shakespeare has no heroes; his scenes are occupied only by men" (Johnson 1765). The other dramatists, as he judged them, raised their persons above the common level of humanity; they furnished them with sentiments which no living man was ever heard to utter, and with a manner of speech contrived rather to exact admiration than to produce belief. Shakespeare declined this practice, and Johnson reckons his declining it among the chief of his merits. The persons of his plays speak as the reader would himself have spoken, had the same situation enclosed him and the same pressure been laid upon him. Their language is taken from the common intercourse of life; and they move us because in them we recognise ourselves. Nor is this true only where the action is probable. A ghost, or a meeting of witches, lies wholly outside experience; but the speech of those who behold such things remains within it. The marvellous belongs to the plot, and the dialogue keeps to life. Hamlet questions the spirit of his father as any son would question a thing so dreadful. Macbeth broods upon the prophecy of the witches as an ambitious man would brood upon the promise of a crown.
